headline: It’s Boom Times for Old TV Shows. New TV, Not So Much.

paragraphs.text: TJ Helmstetter used to watch lots of new TV shows.

These days, though, his streaming habits are stretching into other decades. Mr. Helmstetter, a 42-year-old political consultant who lives in Washington, just streamed for the first time all 275 episodes of “Cheers,” the hit NBC comedy in the 1980s and ’90s. He and his husband also recently watched crime dramas from the 2010s like “Broadchurch” and “Major Crimes.”

Some new shows made the cut, like “Furious,” a police thriller on Hulu. But between professional obligations and being “decision fatigued” amid a sea of streaming options, the bar is getting much higher to start an original series, Mr. Helmstetter said.
“My brain can’t handle something new and I have been in that mode for like the last year or so,” he added.

He is not alone. Viewership for older television series and movies on streaming services has been on a rapid rise in recent years, according to a pair of research firms. Viewership for newer series, not so much.
There are plenty of reasons people are turning to older fare like “Girls,” “Mad Men,” “Glee” and “The West Wing.”

The industry is making significantly fewer scripted and reality series compared with just four years ago, leaving viewers hunting for other content in a post-Peak TV era. Some streamers have been struggling to get audiences to show up for new shows, and an even harder time keeping them there for subsequent seasons.

Netflix, the biggest subscription streamer of them all, recently ousted its top programming leader as it struggles to find new giant hits. And viewers said it is comforting to revisit old classics or finally check them off their watch list.

Back libraries, of course, have long been the backbone of cable television and streaming. Plenty of people have discovered older series in the streaming era, like “Suits,” on Netflix. But now they’re finding them on other apps, like HBO Max, too: “The Big Bang Theory” became the most-watched show in America over the summer, according to Nielsen, even though it has been off the air for seven years.
As viewership for older series rises, it underscores the challenges all studios and entertainment executives are confronting in trying to get new TV shows in front of audiences.

As recently as 2023, original programming accounted for 17 percent of streaming usage, according to Nielsen. For much of the last year, that figure has fallen to 13 percent or lower, despite an overall spike in streaming viewership.

Data from Luminate, another research firm, is even starker: Viewing of library content jumped more than 40 percent among major subscription streaming services in the third quarter this year, compared with the same period of time last year. Viewership for new TV series and movies during the same time period declined modestly.

There are also fewer sustainable new hits this year. According to Nielsen’s weekly streaming ratings charts, an original series drew a total of at least two billion minutes of viewing time in any given week 21 times last year. (That’s the company’s benchmark for a very big hit; “Stranger Things,” “Bridgerton” and “The Lincoln Lawyer” were among the shows that cleared that number.) This year, that figure has dropped to nine.
Other popular distractions, including sporting events, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and video games like Grand Theft Auto VI, could also be playing a role.

Robert Greenblatt, a former top executive at NBC and WarnerMedia and an executive producer of “The Gilded Age,” said that it’s much easier to be a producer for a popular recurring series right now than it is to bring “a whole new show to the marketplace.”

“We’re still being pummeled by new shows on every streaming service and rather than try to figure out what’s worth committing to, it’s easier to just escape into ‘Seinfeld’ or ‘Downton Abbey’ because you know exactly what you’re getting,” he said.
Some viewers have complained it is harder than ever to even discover that a new show exists, something executives describe as a “discoverability” problem.

Emily Bianchi, a 37-year-old who lives outside Detroit, said that despite paying for subscriptions for at least seven streaming services, she has found herself spending most of her viewing time recently with older shows like “Mad Men,” which premiered in 2007 on AMC, and “Dexter,” which debuted in 2006 on Showtime.

“It’s hard to know where to find shows,” she said. “The only social media I’m on is Instagram and Threads and if it’s not popping up on my feed then I really just have no idea. You’re kind of on your own to find that stuff.”

Lisa Baar, a 66-year-old retiree who lives in Virginia Beach, said she and her husband were taken with Damien Lewis’s performance during a recent rewatch of “Band of Brothers,” the 2001 HBO mini-series. That inspired them to watch for the first time another show of his, “Homeland,” which ran on Showtime between 2011 and 2020. They devoured it, and she thought it was better than any new show that she has seen recently.
“We’ll start watching a new show and it never sticks,” she said.

The majority of older TV shows also have far more episodes than newer shows, which gives them a big leg up in viewing time tallies. HBO’s “Succession,” a three-time best drama winner in the 2020s at the Emmy Awards, had all of 39 episodes; “The West Wing,” a four-time winner from the 2000s, had 156. Twenty years ago, “Grey’s Anatomy” used to have 25 episodes a season — this season the episode count is whittled down to 13.

Executives are aware of that imbalance. Casey Bloys, the chief content officer at Skydance’s streaming division and the longtime programming head at HBO, has said that he programmed “The Pitt,” which runs at 15 episodes every season, because of the importance of making shows that future generations can spend dozens of hours with.

“Those libraries are incredibly important and have fueled streaming,” he said in an interview with The New York Times last year. “One of the thoughts we had was, well, if we don’t make new ones, you’re not going to have another library in the future like that.”

John Landgraf, the longtime head of FX, underscored a similar point this year. In July, Mr. Landgraf undertook an unusual experiment and greenlit a new premiere episode to get audiences to give his comedy “Adults” another chance. The show’s viewership figures were low, but he had a feeling it has the potential to be a “Friends” for a future generation.

“Why, as an industry, are we not making more deep library?” he told The Times over the summer. “That seems crazy to me when I can see what our viewers are doing. They’re consuming our deep library. It’s one of our most valuable assets.”

Mr. Helmstetter, and his husband, Mike Naple, said they are not afraid of watching a new show. But they are more deliberate than they used to be. They will often go through a checklist: Who’s starring? Has it been nominated for an Emmy? Which night can they focus and watch, and not have another device out?

“Often times, I’ll be like, ‘All right, we’ve got these new shows that are coming up, I think these are going to be good,’” Mr. Naple said. “And then it’s, like, ‘Well, no, I don’t want to do something new.’ Then we’re watching Season 5 of ‘Project Runway.’”
